subject: English
passage: The deployment of unreliable first-person narrators is well documented in the gothic novel and other works within the broader subgenre of nineteenth-century sensation fiction. An extensive meta-analysis conducted by Jun Han, Adewale Kaplan, and colleagues revealed that this narrative device has appeared across a surprisingly large generic distribution of 14 novelistic subgenres, including epistolary romance and picaresque satire. Subsequent investigation of potential causal factors prompted the researchers to conclude that independent of novelistic subgenre, the prevalence of the device is mediated by sociohistorical conditions associated with the decade of a work's publication.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Across the subgenres in the study, approximately 55% of the works examined were published in decades from 1820 to 1880, but most of the works that are known to employ unreliable first-person narrators were published in decades from 1890 to 1940.
choices.B: Unreliable first-person narrators are documented in sensation fiction works across the entire range of publication decades within that subgenre, but in works from other subgenres, unreliable first-person narrators are documented only when publication occurred 30-40 years later than what is typical for those subgenres.
choices.C: The use of unreliable first-person narrators is widespread in sensation fiction works independent of the decade of publication, but its prevalence in other novelistic subgenres is limited to works published in the decades from 1890 to 1940.
choices.D: Across the subgenres in the study, unreliable first-person narrators are observed in approximately 32% of works published in the decades from 1820 to 1860 and approximately 61% of works published in the decades from 1900 to 1940.

explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it presents a finding that, if true, would most strongly support the researchers' conclusion that the prevalence of unreliable first-person narrators is mediated by the decade of publication independent of novelistic subgenre. The text explains that Han, Kaplan, and colleagues found this device across 14 novelistic subgenres and concluded that sociohistorical conditions associated with publication decade, rather than which subgenre a work belongs to, determine how prevalent the device is. To support this conclusion, evidence would need to show that prevalence correlates with publication decade across all the subgenres studied, not just within particular subgenres. Choice D provides exactly this evidence: across all subgenres in the study, approximately 32% of works published in earlier decades (1820-1860) employ unreliable first-person narrators, while approximately 61% of works published in later decades (1900-1940) employ the device. This clear increase in prevalence with later publication, measured across subgenres rather than within any single subgenre, directly supports the conclusion that publication decade mediates the device's prevalence independent of subgenre.
